md: A VPN is not anonymity and a firewall is not a security boundary for everything. The VPN provider sees what your ISP used to see, and a firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Each control answers one question; know which one.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
md: Simplified model: it ignores caches, assumes perfect overlap, symmetric links and that threads can saturate their controller. Real numbers differ by machine, so measure with your workload. The *ordering* of the options is what the model teaches.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Where candidate boxes come from: proposals, anchors and grids
md: Anchors and grid cells are not predictions. They are fixed reference positions that predictions are expressed relative to. A detector with 20000 anchors does not find 20000 objects; almost all of them are scored as background.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: S3 is not just a slow disk. A disk charges nothing per write and lets you overwrite 4 KiB in place. S3 charges per request, writes whole immutable objects, and takes tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds per request. Every design in this course reshapes writes into **few, large, immutable objects**.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Counts aggregate; quantiles do not. If you want to compute a percentile across instances, regions or time windows later, you must store counts per bucket now. That single decision is why histograms beat summaries almost everywhere.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold
md: Dense text detectors predict a per-pixel map. EAST regresses a box from every text pixel and merges them; DBNet segments shrunk text kernels with a learned threshold, then expands them back.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The reference monitor: one checker that sees every access
md: "We check permissions in the web UI" is not complete mediation. If the API behind the UI, a batch job or a debug endpoint reaches the same data without the check, the monitor is bypassed. Ask of every design: is there any path to the object that skips the checker?

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Virtual machines, containers, gVisor and Firecracker
md: Containers share the host kernel; their strength is the strength of that kernel plus the filters in front of it. VMs give each workload its own kernel and put a small VMM on the boundary. gVisor puts a memory-safe kernel of its own in between. Choose by how untrusted the code is: your own services, other teams' code, or strangers' code.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Search operators: asking a search engine precise questions
md: Run operator searches against your own organisation or a client who has authorised it. Downloading files a search reveals, such as a password list, can itself be unauthorised access or handling of stolen data. Record that the result exists and report it.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Chronolocation: telling the time from shadows
md: Shadow length gives the sun's elevation, shadow direction gives its azimuth, and an astronomical calculation turns both into a time window for a known place and date.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
md: Rebuild cost is decided by the include graph. Touching a header recompiles every translation unit that reaches it, directly or transitively. That is why big projects keep widely included headers small and stable.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
md: A red X on one matrix cell with grey cancelled cells next to it does not mean the other platforms passed. With fail-fast they never finished. Look at which job failed first; that is the one with the real log.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
md: Never reply in anger. Google's guide calls it a serious breach of etiquette that lives forever in the review tool. If a comment stings, ask what constructive point the reviewer is making, and answer that point once you are calm.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Issue first: when to ask, how to report, how to claim work
md: Closing keywords (`close`, `closes`, `closed`, `fix`, `fixes`, `fixed`, `resolve`, `resolves`, `resolved`) only work when the PR targets the repository's **default branch**. Aimed at a release or feature branch, the keyword is ignored and the issue stays open after merge.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebasing replays your commits on a new base. Every replayed commit gets a new hash because its parent changed, even if its diff is identical.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: A license is permission plus conditions. The conditions only apply when you do the thing they attach to, which for most licenses means distributing the code.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
md: A performance claim is an experiment. The PR must let a reviewer rerun it (exact commands, setup, commits) and weigh it (spread, significance and costs), not just read a headline number.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Search that narrows: git grep, ripgrep and word matches
md: GitHub's "find references" is name-based: the docs say it searches all definitions and references across a repository "to find entities with a given name". Two unrelated functions with the same name in different modules will both show up. Check the file and its imports before you trust a reference.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Delta debugging: let a script shrink the repro
md: Automated reduction needs only a yes or no oracle, a check that gives the verdict: does this candidate still show the exact failure? Write that test carefully and the tool does the tedious part.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: Each PR (and each commit in a series) should be justifiable on its own and leave the project building and passing tests. If one depends on another, say so in the description.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Sharing blocks with reference counts and copy-on-write
md: A physical block may back many logical blocks. Reference counts say when it can be freed; copy-on-write makes writes into shared blocks safe, at the cost of copying one block.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: what your DNS tells the world
md: Recon results drive scope questions, not actions. Finding that `vpn.example.com` exists does not make it in scope. Check the address against the scope guard before any active step.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: From perf.data to folded stacks
md: In `perf report`, a high Children value does not mean the function is doing the work. main is 100% in every program. Sort by Self to find what executes, by Children to find which caller to change.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Visibility and durability are different events. A store becomes visible when it reaches the coherent cache, and durable only when its line reaches the persistence domain. On ADR platforms, software must close that gap explicitly.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: SPF: which servers may send for a domain
md: Misconception: "SPF pass means the sender is who they claim". SPF pass means only that the connecting IP is allowed to send for the **envelope** domain. That domain may be the attacker's own.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
md: Which end of a storage unit bit-fields start from, whether they may straddle units, and the signedness of a plain `int` bit-field are all implementation-defined in C (cppreference lists them). Two compilers or two ABIs can lay out the same bit-field struct differently, so never use bit-fields to match a wire format or a hardware register; use shifts and masks on a fixed-width integer instead.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A pose model's output is a fixed, ordered list of keypoints per person, each with a position and a confidence. Everything downstream (metrics, angles, rep counting) is arithmetic on that list.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Do not read 3% as a safe threshold. Proximity graphs are not random graphs, matching nodes are often clustered, and being connected is weaker than being *navigable*: greedy search can stall in a matching region long before the subgraph formally splits. Qdrant's docs simply warn that the HNSW graph starts to fall apart when filters are too strict.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: What privacy engineering protects, beyond keeping secrets
md: "Encrypted, access-controlled and never breached" is a security result, not a privacy result. A system can meet every confidentiality control and still harm people through what it does by design with the data: publishing, combining, inferring or keeping it.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: k-anonymity: generalise and suppress until you hide in a crowd
md: k-anonymity: every combination of quasi-identifier values appears at least k times, achieved by generalising and suppressing. Its strength depends entirely on choosing the right quasi-identifiers and on every other release made from the same data.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy in real systems: units, trust and hazards
md: Check every DP claim for its unit of privacy (event or user), its trust model (central, local or in between), its epsilon and delta (delta at most 1 / n squared), and its implementation (a vetted library, not hand-written noise).

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Secure aggregation: a server that learns only the sum
md: Secure aggregation: pairwise masks that cancel in the sum hide each value from the server; secret sharing handles dropouts; double masking stops a server from faking dropouts. The total is still revealed, so require many contributors and add DP noise when the total must not identify anyone.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 2: jobs, scripts and paths that root trusts
md: The same rule covers the files that define privilege themselves. A writable `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers.d/` entry or systemd unit directory is instant root. Treat any group or world write bit under `/etc` or `/usr` as a finding.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Build it: train a small PRM and rerank with it
md: Tokenize each step separately and append the separator id yourself. In the Qwen2.5 tokenizer a step ending in a period followed by a newline becomes the single token for period-plus-newline (id 624), so tokenizing the joined text gives no separate newline token to read, and the label would sit on a different token than at training time.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a process owns and what a thread shares
md: A process is a **resource container** (memory, files, handlers); a thread is an **execution stream** (PC, registers, stack). Threads in one process see each other's writes; separate processes do not, unless they set up sharing on purpose.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: The one number to remember is not the microseconds of a single switch but **switches per second times total cost per switch**, where total includes the cache and TLB refill. Keep CPU-bound threads near the core count, and reserve extra threads or async I/O for work that actually waits.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Worked example: selecting a prompt and the winner's curse
md: The data that chose the prompt cannot also grade it. Report the selected prompt's score on a held-out set that played no part in any choice, and expect it to be lower than the dev score.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Text versus bytes: what a computer actually stores
md: Do not "fix" decode errors with `errors="ignore"` in security tooling. It silently deletes the bad bytes, so `ad\xffmin` becomes `admin` and your report shows a username the attacker never sent. Prefer `replace`, which leaves a visible mark.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
md: Never decode and then *run* what you decoded to see what it does. Decode to text, read it, and search it. Executing an unknown PowerShell or shell command, even in your own terminal, is how an analyst becomes the next victim. Use an isolated analysis sandbox if you truly need behaviour.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: Rocchio, pseudo-relevance feedback and RM3
md: Feedback is only as good as its top k. When the first-pass top results are relevant, PRF finds words the user never typed; when they are off-topic, it amplifies the error. On MS MARCO dev, the query2doc paper reports BM25 MRR@10 18.4 against 15.8 for BM25 + RM3, while recall@1k rose slightly (85.7 to 86.4).

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: The rotation does not make every vector quantize well on every draw. It makes the quality *random with a known distribution*, the same for every input direction. That is what turns "works on my dataset" into a guarantee that holds regardless of the data.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Discounts, refunds and rewards: value that can be claimed twice
md: Evaluate every reward rule against the final state of the transaction, at the moment value moves, and record each grant so it cannot be granted again. A rule checked earlier is a rule that can go stale.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Fixing races in the database: atomic updates, locks, constraints
md: "It is in a transaction" is not a race fix by itself. At Read Committed, a SELECT then an UPDATE in one transaction still race. You need a lock, a conditional write, a constraint, or SERIALIZABLE with retries.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Why replicas need consensus, and why majorities work
md: Majorities intersect. Every safety argument in Paxos and Raft comes down to one server that sat in both quorums and remembered what it saw.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Top-k, the token budget, and where chunks sit in the prompt
md: Three separate decisions shape the context: **how many** chunks (top-k), **how many tokens** they may use (the budget, set by the window minus everything else), and **in what order** they appear. Tune them together; raising k without a budget or an ordering rule mostly adds noise to the middle.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: **Recall@k is not Success@k.** Some papers report "Recall@k" meaning *at least one relevant document is in the top k*. The ir_measures documentation calls that **Success@k** and reserves R@k for the fraction of all relevant documents retrieved. For q1 every run has Success@5 = 1, while R@5 ranges from 0.167 to 0.667. Check which one a paper means before comparing numbers.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Extortion layers: encryption, theft, leak sites and pressure
md: Backups defeat encryption only. Stolen data is lost the moment it leaves, so treat exfiltration detection as part of ransomware defence, and prepare the communication that answers a leak-site post before one appears.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Recovery sequencing: identity first, then the business
md: Recover in dependency order: a clean network, then the independent backup system, then identity restored in isolation from a pre-attack backup with privileged secrets reset, then security tooling, then business services by a critical asset list agreed before the incident.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
md: Masking is **not encryption**: the key travels in the same frame. RFC 6455 requires it (even over TLS) so that a script in the browser cannot choose the exact bytes on the wire. Without it, an attacker could craft upgraded traffic that a broken proxy reads as an HTTP request and caches, then serves that forged response to other users: the cache-poisoning attack in section 10.3. Use `wss://` (TLS) for confidentiality.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Item-to-item CF scales because the heavy work (the similar-items table) is offline, and the online step only touches the handful of items in one user's history.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why a photo has no scale until you add a reference
md: A reference object gives you scale only for points at its depth (more precisely, on its plane). Everything else in the image has a different pixels-per-mm.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The same study found that most of PostgreSQL's timeouts came from a nested-loop join without an index, chosen because a tiny row estimate made it look cheapest. When the real input was large, its rows x rows work exploded. A cost-only choice ignores how risky a plan is if the estimate is wrong.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: The reward is an imperfect measurement of the goal. Optimization pressure flows to wherever the measurement and the goal disagree, so the harder you optimize, the more those disagreements decide what you get.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
md: Multiplying ordinal numbers (ranks, like 1 to 5) treats the gap between 4 and 5 as equal to the gap between 1 and 2, which is rarely true of real losses. Grids are fine for sorting a long list quickly and for talking to non-specialists. They are not fine for deciding whether a USD 300,000 control is worth buying. For that, estimate in money.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, profiles and tiers
md: Misconception: "we implemented the CSF". The CSF lists outcomes, not controls; you cannot install it. Saying you *use* it means you have profiles, owners for the gaps and a review cycle. A slide with the six function names is not alignment.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Compliance as code: policy checks in CI and automatic evidence
md: A control that runs as code on every change is both stronger security and better evidence: the CI logs show it ran on every pull request all year, and the evidence store shows the state on any date an auditor picks. Failing the build is the cheapest moment to fix a compliance gap.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Cyber insurance transfers part of the financial tail: forensics, restoration, business interruption, liability. It is priced and conditioned on your controls; misstatements can void claims. Model deductible and limit against your loss distribution, read the exclusions (fraud, war and state-backed attacks), and keep the application as true as your SOC 2.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: Sync cost = bytes / bandwidth + resharding. The bytes are fixed by model size and precision; good systems avoid gathering the full model anywhere, send each rank only its shard, and keep the transfer off the critical path.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
md: Correlation is not causation, and the SRE troubleshooting chapter names the two ways this bites. First, correlated events often share a cause: packet loss in a cluster and failed disks in the same cluster correlate because a power event hit both, not because either caused the other. Second, as you monitor more metrics it becomes inevitable that some will correlate well with your symptom purely by coincidence.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Ties, missing documents and the window size
md: Pagination: in Elasticsearch, if `from + size` (results skipped plus the page length) exceeds `rank_window_size` you get 0 results, and pages are only consistent while `rank_window_size` stays fixed. Changing W re-ranks everything, as the animation shows, so never vary it between page requests.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
md: The pattern is always the same: an `unsafe` C protocol (lock and unlock, get and put, register and unregister) becomes a value whose constructor does the first half and whose `Drop` does the second. The type system then tracks the protocol for every caller.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: A CPU only ever runs tasks from its own local DSQ. Everything else (global DSQ, custom DSQs, BPF maps) is staging. The pick order is local, then global, then `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
md: Placement is decided when a task lands in a local DSQ. `select_cpu` and the idle cpumask choose where, `LOCAL_ON` puts it there from any CPU, and kicks (`IDLE`, `PREEMPT`) decide when that CPU looks.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Secrets: what they are, how long they live, why they sprawl
md: A secret's danger is what it opens, times how long it works, times how many places it lives. Every technique in this course shrinks one of those three: least privilege shrinks the first, rotation and dynamic secrets the second, vaults and scanning the third.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: The end state: workload identity instead of stored secrets
md: The best secret is one that does not exist at rest. Where one must exist, make it short-lived, unique to one consumer, held in one audited place and rotated automatically with overlap.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
md: Any code that writes `obj[key] = value` with a key from input, or walks nested input recursively, must refuse `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`, or use objects with no prototype. Any string that reaches eval, Function or a string timer is code injection.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Compiler warnings and hardening flags a C reviewer should demand
md: Warnings find bugs; hardening flags limit the damage of the bugs you missed. Review build files like code: a change that removes either, or adds -Wno-format-security or -fno-stack-protector, needs the same scrutiny as a change to authentication.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec building blocks: SAs, SPIs, ESP, AH and two modes
md: A common misconception: tunnel mode is not more encrypted than transport mode. Both use the same ESP encryption. Tunnel mode additionally hides the inner addresses and lets a gateway protect traffic for a whole network; transport mode is for two hosts protecting their own traffic.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Encrypting email itself: S/MIME, OpenPGP and EFAIL (2018)
md: EFAIL's root cause was releasing unauthenticated plaintext into an active renderer (HTML that fetches URLs). Authenticated encryption plus a strict rule (verify first, show nothing on failure) removes the gadget attack; disabling remote content in the client removes the easiest exfiltration channel.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Inside BeyondCorp: inventory, trust tiers and the access proxy
md: In an access-proxy design the device inventory and the identity system are part of the trusted computing base. If the inventory says a stolen laptop is healthy, every check downstream agrees.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: From a script to a pipeline: the parts of a security automation
md: A security automation is a small distributed system that holds powerful credentials and processes data attackers can influence. Design for duplicates, partial failure and hostile input from the first version.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Measuring AI triage: golden sets, precision, recall and attack success
md: Golden-set labels must come from completed investigations. If you label with first-look verdicts, you measure how well the model copies hurried humans, including their misses.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who attacks and why: criminals, states, insiders, activists
md: Ask "who would want this asset, and what would they do with it?" Criminals want quick money and reuse easy entry points such as stolen passwords. States want long, quiet access. Insiders already have access. The defence emphasis differs for each, but removing unused access helps against all of them.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
md: Kill chain: seven phases, and breaking any link stops the intrusion. ATT&CK: tactics (why) and techniques (how) with IDs, the shared language of detection rules and threat reports.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Risk memos and exceptions: making someone own the decision
md: An exception is a decision with a name, a reason, compensating controls and an end date. Without all four it is just an unfixed vulnerability that someone has stopped looking at.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
md: Each STaR iteration fine-tunes the **original** pretrained model on the new dataset, not the previous checkpoint, to avoid overfitting. ReST-EM does the same and reports much better transfer to held-out tasks than continuing from the last iteration. The model improves through better data, not through stacked training runs.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Compression has costs of its own. The compressor runs on the critical path of every request. The compressed text is hard for humans to read, which makes debugging and audits harder. Exact strings (code, JSON, numbers, IDs) can be damaged by token deletion. And question-aware compression produces a different context for every question, so that context can no longer be served from the provider's prefix cache.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell: how logging a string ran code
md: Only `log4j-core` 2.x is affected; applications with just `log4j-api` are not, and Log4j 1.x has no lookups (its separate JMSAppender issue is CVE-2021-4104). But Log4j is often a *transitive* dependency: a library you use pulls it in, so "we do not use Log4j" needs checking, not assuming.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
md: Cache locality and load balance pull against each other. Sending every request of a hot prefix to one worker maximizes hits and can overload that worker; the balance thresholds exist to break locality when queues diverge. The gateway's trees are approximate: they are inferred from routed text, not read from the workers, so they can be stale.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: No technique wins on every axis. Look at query time, preprocessing time, memory, how quickly new traffic weights can be applied, and whether turns and other metrics are supported. A static fastest-route server and a live-traffic service often choose differently.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
md: Every hand-written SIMD loop has a vector body, a horizontal reduction and a tail. A vector reduction adds in a different order than the scalar loop, so float results can change, which is why compilers need permission to reassociate.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: "Arena" means different things in different allocators. In this lesson it is a bump region freed all at once. In jemalloc (a general-purpose malloc used by FreeBSD and Firefox, among others) and in glibc malloc (the GNU C library's allocator, the default on most Linux systems) an *arena* is an independent general-purpose heap with its own locks, used so threads contend less; you still free objects one by one there.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
md: The colocated code keeps a comment worth remembering: SGLang returns from the update request after enqueueing GPU copies, not after they finish. Reusing the same flattened IPC buffer for the next bucket right away could overwrite memory SGLang is still reading and corrupt weights, so slime allocates a fresh buffer per bucket.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Enrichment: asset, identity and intel context, and where it lies
md: Enrichment answers "what is this thing?", not "is this bad?". Treat every enriched field as a claim with a source and an age, show unknowns explicitly, and never let a single reputation score close or escalate an alert by itself.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Talking to users, owners and leaders during an investigation
md: Never let an attacker-controlled message decide who you trust. A chat message saying "I'm from IT, please approve the prompt" is exactly what the Lapsus$ actors sent, per the CSRB. The same rule applies inside the SOC: verify urgent requests to disable monitoring or grant access through a second channel.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Designing help-desk verification that holds under pressure
md: Misconception: "on-camera verification solves help-desk fraud". It raises the bar, but synthetic video and stolen ID images are already used against identity checks (FinCEN, 2024). Pair it with an out-of-band confirmation for anything privileged, and keep the most powerful admin accounts out of help-desk reach entirely.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: An SAE is dictionary learning with a neural network: an encoder that picks a few latents, a decoder whose columns are the dictionary directions, and a loss that trades reconstruction against sparsity.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Every interpolator here is a weighted average $\sum_i \lambda_i z_i$. The only question is how to pick the weights. Keep this frame: the rest of the course compares weight recipes on the same six sensors.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Kriging is the best linear unbiased predictor (linear: a weighted sum of readings; unbiased: weights sum to 1; best: smallest error variance) only under its own model. With few points, an unreliable variogram can make it worse than IDW, as in this toy. Its variance map is only as trustworthy as the variogram, so check calibration with standardized LOO errors.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts, prompt lookup, and speculation in vLLM
md: All variants share one loop: draft cheaply (small model, extra heads, feature-level head, or string lookup), verify a chain or tree in one target pass, keep the accepted prefix plus one target token. They differ only in how they guess, and that sets alpha and c.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The map of a process: segments, /proc/PID/maps and ASLR
md: A big line in `/proc/PID/maps` is not memory in use. A VMA only says which addresses the program may touch; Linux's memory concepts docs note that anonymous mappings usually just define those areas, and physical pages arrive on first access. A 1 GiB mapping that was never written uses almost no RAM.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
md: A miss does not always cost four DRAM reads. The page-table entries are ordinary data that can sit in the CPU caches, and Linux's page-table docs note that MMUs also keep page walk caches for upper levels. The four loads are the worst case of the structure, not a fixed latency.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
md: A steering vector edits **activations**, not weights and not the prompt. It is computed once, before inference, and the same vector is added on every forward pass while it is switched on.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Watermark = the processor's estimate of how far event time has progressed. It decides when a window first fires; allowed lateness decides how long the window can still be corrected; anything beyond is dropped or side-output. Every choice trades latency for completeness.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, teacher forcing and cross-attention
md: A causal mask sets the scores of future positions to minus infinity before softmax, so with teacher forcing every target position trains in one pass without seeing its own answer. Cross-attention is the same function with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: "Transformer" does not mean "GPT" (generative pre-trained transformer, OpenAI's line of decoder-only language models). The 2017 model is an encoder-decoder for translation. Decoder-only language models keep only its masked self-attention stack; encoder-only models keep only the unmasked encoder.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
md: Training is **teacher forcing on every position in parallel**: the true previous tokens are always the context, and all $B \times T$ predictions are scored in one pass. Generation is the opposite, one token at a time feeding its own outputs back in.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
md: The model never stores the text it generated anywhere except in `idx`. There is no hidden memory across calls: anything older than `block_size` tokens is simply cropped away and cannot influence the next prediction.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
md: The gradient points in the direction of **steepest ascent**, and its length is that steepest rate. So $-\nabla f$ is the direction of steepest descent, the direction every gradient-based **optimizer** (the algorithm that updates the parameters during training) starts from.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation: the chain rule run backward through a graph
md: Gradient checks can fail for honest reasons: at a kink (a sharp corner) such as ReLU at 0 (lesson 2) or a max with ties, the function is not differentiable and the two sides disagree. Check at random points away from kinks, and in double precision.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
md: Misconception: `2>&1` *links* stderr to stdout permanently. It does not. It is a one-time copy of fd 1 as it is at that moment. Any later change to fd 1 leaves fd 2 where it was.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Job control and signals: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, background jobs and trap
md: Ctrl-C is SIGINT, Ctrl-Z is SIGTSTP, `kill` is SIGTERM, `kill -9` is SIGKILL, and a closed terminal is SIGHUP. In a script, route every way out, signals included, through one `trap ... EXIT` cleanup.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Evaluating and visualizing an embedding space
md: A t-SNE plot shows neighbourhoods, not geometry. Do not conclude that one cluster is more varied than another, or that two clusters are closer than a third, from the picture. Check such claims with distances computed in the original space.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Doubling peak TFLOP/s does almost nothing for batch-1 decode. What helps is moving fewer bytes per token (smaller or quantized weights: quantizing stores each weight in fewer bits, so 8-bit weights halve the bytes) or using each byte for more tokens (batching, next lessons).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
md: Misconception: "signed overflow wraps in C too." The hardware adder wraps, but in C, overflowing a signed integer is [undefined behavior](https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/language/operator_arithmetic), and compilers optimize on the assumption that it never happens. Only unsigned arithmetic is guaranteed to wrap modulo $2^n$.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
md: Performance is often decided by memory access patterns, not instruction counts. Touch memory sequentially, reuse data while it is still in cache, and keep hot data small.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline
md: Raw crawl becomes training data through extraction, filtering, near-duplicate removal, PII and contamination handling, then packing. Each step was chosen by training small models on the result, and a run then moves through stages: main pretraining, context extension, annealing.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
md: RLHF does not maximize reward. It maximizes reward minus beta times the KL from the SFT model, and beta sets how far the model may move to chase the reward model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
md: The vector space model scores a document by the cosine between its tf-idf vector and the query's. Engines compute it by streaming the query terms' postings into accumulators, so documents that share no query term cost nothing.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Multi-file C: headers, include guards, static, extern and make
md: Headers hold declarations (`extern` variables, prototypes) behind an include guard; exactly one .c file holds each definition; `static` keeps helpers private. A Makefile lists what each file depends on, and make rebuilds only what is older than its inputs.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Before you keep a pointer, ask how long the object behind it lives. Locals die when their function returns, malloc'd memory dies at free, and realloc can retire the old address at any call.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
md: Develop C with `-Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined` on, and fix every warning. Most of the pointer and lifetime bugs from this course then fail loudly at the exact line instead of corrupting memory silently.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: Shared XOR mutable: any number of `&T`, or exactly one `&mut T`, never both at the same point in the program. A borrow is live from creation to last use.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
md: Default to borrowing; move when the callee should keep the value; clone when copies are cheap or necessary; use `Rc`/`RefCell` only for data with genuinely shared ownership.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: $A\mathbf{x}$ is both a stack of dot products (one per row) and a weighted sum of columns. The columns of $A$ are the images of the basis vectors, so they fully describe the map.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Tensors, batches and broadcasting: shapes in real code
md: Broadcasting checks sizes, never meaning. A loss computed from (3, 1) predictions and (3,) targets averages 9 differences instead of 3 and raises nothing. Assert shapes where arrays from different places meet: `assert pred.shape == y.shape`.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
md: With many features, predictions are $\hat y = Xw$ and the MSE gradient is $\frac{2}{n}X^\top(Xw - y)$. Its minimum solves the normal equations $X^\top Xw = X^\top y$. Features on very different scales stretch the bowl, so gradient descent crawls; standardizing them rounds it out.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Validation and penalties: choosing lambda, L2 and L1
md: Choose capacity and penalty strength by **validation** error and keep the test set for one final check. L2 (weight decay) shrinks every weight a little each step; L1 pins weak weights at exactly zero and so selects features.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: Misconception: a deeper network of linear layers is more expressive. It is not; it is exactly as expressive as one linear layer. Another one: universal approximation means any network will learn any function. It only guarantees that suitable weights exist.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradients through depth: vanishing, exploding and unlucky seeds
md: Backprop computes the exact gradient of the loss at the current weights; it does not guarantee a good solution. The loss surface of a network is not **convex** (bowl-shaped, so that every valley is the lowest one), so the starting point matters. Lesson: always check the loss curve, and try more than one seed.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
md: Memory is a cache for pages, and a disk-backed miss costs about 100,000 memory accesses. A replacement policy tries to approximate OPT using the past: LRU in principle, the use bit and the clock algorithm in practice, preferring clean pages.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: how a hard disk spends its time
md: A random disk I/O is almost all positioning: seek plus half a rotation, milliseconds, against microseconds of transfer. Make requests large and sequential, and let the scheduler order them by position.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Conditioning means restricting attention to the outcomes consistent with what you know, then renormalizing so they sum to 1. Almost every formula in this course is that one idea applied carefully.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
md: Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and sunburns are correlated because sunny weather drives both: a **confounder**, a third variable that causes both. The Deep Learning textbook by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville makes the same point about conditioning: P(from Germany | speaks German) is high, but teaching someone German does not change where they are from.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
md: Power depends on the effect size you assume. Choose the smallest effect worth acting on before you see data, not the effect you hope for and not the effect a finished test happened to show.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
md: A scaling study is an experiment design problem: budgets spread over orders of magnitude, sizes that bracket each valley, a properly ended schedule per run, then two fits (IsoFLOP parabolas and the parametric form) that should agree, each with bootstrap error bars.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
md: nDCG@k answers: what fraction of the best achievable discounted gain did the top k results capture? It is the default when labels are graded and users look mostly at the first page.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
md: Each stage covers another's blind spot: BM25 for rare exact terms, the bi-encoder for meaning across different words, the cross-encoder for precise final ordering on a short list. Evaluate the whole pipeline on your own queries with a metric such as recall at k (the share of relevant passages that appear in the top k results).

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Build a byte-level BPE tokenizer in Python
md: Decode with `errors="replace"` (or keep bytes) whenever ids can be cut at arbitrary points: one token at a time while streaming, or a sequence the model generated that may not be valid UTF-8. With strict decoding a partial character raises an error. When streaming, keep the bytes and only show the characters once all their bytes have arrived.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Residual connections: why 56 layers trained worse than 20
md: A residual block computes $x + F(x)$. The identity path makes doing nothing easy to learn and gives the gradient a direct route to every layer. Start each branch near zero so that a deep stack begins as one identity map rather than a variance amplifier.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude fewer distance computations. Every ANN number you read (or report) should come as a pair: recall@k and speed, measured against exact brute-force results on the same queries.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Version ranges and lockfiles: why new code arrives unasked
md: A lockfile only protects installs that use it. A Dockerfile that copies only package.json, `npx some-tool`, a global install, or a developer running `npm update` all resolve ranges fresh. The axios post-mortem told users who were "pinned to a clean version" and ran no fresh install in the window that they were fine.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
md: The xz attack was a trust attack, not a technical exploit of git, signing or builds. Every step was done by a legitimate maintainer with legitimate rights. Defences are partly social: fund and share maintenance of critical projects, add second reviewers for releases, and treat sudden pressure to hand over control or upgrade fast as a warning sign.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
md: Synthetic data are useful when an outside signal decides what is kept, diversity is designed in, and real data stay in the training mix. Model collapse is what happens when all three are missing.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR
md: Every `read` and `write` may block, move fewer bytes than asked, or fail with `EINTR` or `EAGAIN`. Loop until all bytes are moved, retry on `EINTR`, and treat `EAGAIN` as "wait until the descriptor is ready".

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
md: strace shows which calls a program makes and how often; getrusage shows the page faults that strace cannot see; seccomp turns a list of needed calls into an enforced allow-list. All three work on syscall numbers and miss the vDSO.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
md: A relative expression has no value until it is anchored. *Present*, *now*, *today*, *last year* and *the past 5 years* all need a reference date, and the normalizer should receive it as an explicit input, never read a hidden clock or let a model guess it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
md: Coverage is an **upper bound** on accuracy. It equals real accuracy only if you have a perfect checker (unit tests, a proof checker). For a math word problem, pass@100 = 83% means 83% of problems have *some* correct sample, not that you can find it.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
md: TTT here does not mean fine-tuning the LLM on your prompt. The network's ordinary parameters stay frozen at inference. Only the small per-layer weights $W$ change, they start from $W_0$ for every sequence, and they are discarded afterwards, just like an RNN's hidden state.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
md: A shared lock caps allocator throughput at $1/c$ no matter how many cores you add. The fix is not a faster lock but keeping the common path on state that only one CPU (or thread) touches, and going to shared state rarely and in batches.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Stacking: let the rare thing rise to the top
md: Rare is not malicious and common is not safe. PEAK: "Just because something is abnormal doesn't mean it's malicious." And an attacker who pushes the same tool to every machine at once (ransomware deployment through a management tool, a compromised software update) is not rare at all. Stacking finds the start of an intrusion well and its widespread final stage poorly.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Collection: where intelligence comes from, and what it is worth
md: Collect against requirements, prefer sources about you (internal telemetry, sector peers), and measure every external source by what it contributes: relevance, timeliness and unique hits, not volume. For a question like PIR-1, check CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue from *Security from zero* first.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Attribution: levels, evidence and its limits
md: Technical evidence shows *what* and often *where*: tools, infrastructure, keyboard layouts, working hours. It rarely shows *who pays*. Be wary of attribution that rests on one artefact, on a tool many groups use, or on a country's motive alone, and never copy another vendor's attribution into your report without its confidence and basis.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Ranking threats: risk, DREAD and why it fell out of favour
md: Ranking is a conversation, not a calculation. Use a simple scale, write down the reasons behind each rating, and make sure every threat ends with an explicit response: mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Promotion: finding hot pages trapped in slow memory
md: Promotion needs two signals: *is this page hot* (recency of access) and *can we afford to move it* (free space, rate limit). Missing either one turns tiering into a migration storm.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
md: TLS gives you an encrypted, tamper-evident channel to **whoever holds the private key for a certificate naming that host**. Everything else (is that the right host, is the CA trustworthy, is the code bug-free) is a separate question.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: HSTS, preloading and why key pinning fell out of favour
md: Mobile apps still pin. If you pin, pin to more than one key (RFC 7469 itself required a backup pin), prefer pinning a CA or intermediate key you control over a leaf, have a way to ship new pins before old keys retire, and remember that pinning cannot help against bugs like goto fail, where the chain is genuine but the handshake signature is never checked.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
md: Triton moves the hard parts of a CUDA kernel (coalescing, shared memory, barriers, pipelining) into the compiler, and leaves you the decisions that need knowledge of the problem: the tiling, the program-to-tile order, the masks, and a short list of configs to autotune.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
md: A unikernel is **one application plus only the OS code it uses, linked into one image that boots directly on a hypervisor**. The hypervisor, not a guest kernel, is the isolation boundary.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Paravirtual I/O up close: one packet through a virtqueue
md: A virtqueue is **three shared arrays and two counters**. Data moves through memory for free; only **notifications** cost VM exits and interrupts, so batching, suppression and polling set the price of each packet.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: Deleting from hnswlib with `markDelete` only sets a flag. The node keeps its edges and is still used for routing; it is just filtered out of results. Lots of deletions therefore still cost traversal time until the index is rebuilt.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: 3D-HybridEngine: resharding the actor with zero redundancy
md: The paper describes the mechanism; today's code path is different in detail. With `actor_rollout_ref.hybrid_engine: true`, verl colocates actor and rollout, and the rollout is a vLLM or SGLang server with its own TP. After generation it sleeps (frees KV cache and weights); `update_weights` then wakes the weight memory, streams parameters tensor by tensor from the training engine, and finally restores the KV cache.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
md: In an ST-transformer the dominant cost, spatial attention, scales **linearly** with the number of frames instead of quadratically. That is what lets Genie use spatiotemporal context in the tokenizer, the latent action model and the dynamics model.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: The recipe: schedule, augmentation, per-layer learning rates
md: Augmentation is a training-time tool. At evaluation use only the checkpoint's deterministic resize, center crop and normalization; random crops or Mixup at test time just add noise to your accuracy estimate.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Why a transformer wants an image as a few discrete tokens
md: A visual tokenizer is to images what BPE is to text: a fixed map from raw input to a short sequence of ids from a finite vocabulary. Unlike BPE it is a learned, lossy neural network, so its reconstruction quality caps how good generated images can look.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
md: Automatic selection takes the first backend in the platform's priority list that passes `validate_configuration`. Explicit selection validates one backend and fails loudly. Neither path guesses.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
md: Resolution is the main lever for reading text. Fixed-size models downscale, AnyRes adds tiles up to a grid limit, and dynamic-resolution models spend tokens in proportion to pixels. In every case more legible pixels means more visual tokens.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
md: The hierarchy is about deterministic wait-free algorithms. Herlihy notes that if the guarantee may be probabilistic (finite *expected* steps), the hierarchy collapses: randomized consensus from atomic registers exists. And a high consensus number says nothing about speed; it only says what is possible.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: RMSE rewards hedging. A smooth forecast that predicts the average of possible futures can beat a sharp, realistic one on RMSE while looking nothing like real weather. Read RMSE wins alongside ACC, spectra (how much variation a field has at each spatial scale; a blurry forecast is missing the small scales) or probabilistic scores.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Beyond port 443: what FTP, SMB, SNMP, LDAP and SMTP give away
md: Enumeration is asking questions a stranger should not get answers to. Use safe scripts, get written approval for intrusive ones, and pair every answer with its configuration fix: anonymous off, signing required, SNMPv3, VRFY disabled.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Case: Uber 2016, when a bug bounty was used to hide a breach
md: Authorisation is judged at the moment of access. A policy published afterwards, an NDA or a bounty payment cannot make earlier unauthorised access legal, for the person who took the data or for the company that tries to relabel it.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: CORS: how a server opts in to cross-origin reads
md: CORS is enforced by **browsers**, about **reading**. It is not access control on your server. `curl` or a script outside a browser ignores it completely, and a simple request reaches your server even when the browser will later hide the response. Authentication and authorization still have to happen on the server for every request.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Accounts, groups and SIDs: how Windows names every identity
md: SIDs, not names, are what Windows checks. A renamed Administrator still has RID 500, and a deleted and re-created account gets a new SID, so it does not inherit the old account's permissions.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WPA2: from passphrase to PMK to the 4-way handshake
md: Messages 1 and 2 move the nonces; messages 3 and 4 deliver the group key and confirm the keys, which is also how the handshake protects against downgrades. The PMK itself never crosses the air, but everything else that goes into the PTK does.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app storage: secrets on disk and in the package
md: Obfuscating a hardcoded secret (splitting it, XORing it, hiding it in native code) only slows an analyst down; the app must reconstruct it to use it, so an attacker with the app can too. If a value must stay secret from users, it must not be in the app.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
md: The searching count throttles wakeups, and the barrier on both sides of it prevents lost ones. Remove the throttle and you get a thundering herd; remove the barrier and you get stranded tasks with idle cores.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
md: Zero-copy does not mean faster for every request. It removes per-byte work but adds per-call and per-page bookkeeping. For small messages the copy is cheap and the bookkeeping can cost more, as lesson 5 measures.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: NLI entailment: is the label a true statement about the text?
md: A multi_label score near 0.6 is not a 60% chance the label applies. It is the entailment share after throwing away the neutral mass, from a model trained on MNLI sentence pairs, not on your labels. Treat it as a ranking score and set thresholds on labeled data.
